directions.title: Playground Movers
directions.big_idea: We use pushes and pulls to make things move, and we can design a playground toy that moves the way we want.

lisc.intention: To design and build a moving toy for a playground using pushes and pulls.
criteria: show a push and a pull with my body and with a toy
say which way a push or a pull will move something
plan, build and share a toy that moves with a push or a pull

assessment.title: Book Creator page
assessment.how: Each pair adds a photo of their toy and says push or pull into the page; check against the success criteria.

assessment.title: Observation checklist
assessment.how: Tick the class list as students show a push and a pull with their toy.

assessment.title: Toy showcase
assessment.how: Pairs demonstrate to another pair; listen for push and pull words.

arc.title: Push or Pull?
arc.summary: Move our bodies and classroom objects, and sort actions into pushes and pulls.

arc.title: Push and Pull Detectives
arc.summary: Spot pushes and pulls around the playground and photograph them on the iPad.

arc.title: Big Push, Small Push
arc.summary: Use LEGO and a ramp to see that a bigger push moves things further.

arc.title: Which Way?
arc.summary: Predict and test which way a toy moves when pushed or pulled.

arc.title: Plan a Mover
arc.summary: Draw and label a plan for a toy that moves with a push or a pull.

arc.title: Build a Mover
arc.summary: Build the toy from LEGO and craft materials.

arc.title: Test and Improve
arc.summary: Test the toy, record a short video on the iPad and change one thing.

arc.title: Playground Showcase
arc.summary: Share toys and add a photo and voice recording to a Book Creator page.

resources.why: Building the moving toys and ramps.
Photos, short videos and voice recordings.
One page per pair to show the toy and say push or pull.

connections.how: Pushing, pulling and moving in play links to the physical activity and movement the class already does.
Students listen to and describe sounds and movement, for example a fast push and a slow pull, as a short sound or rhythm.

pedagogy.how: Students plan, build, test and improve a toy to meet a moving goal.
Push, pull, faster and slower are taught and used in every lesson.
Photos and drawings carry the ideas, with few words.
Lessons 5 and 6 model one plan and one build before pairs start.

backbone: Move from the body to objects to a built toy, concrete before abstract.
Teach push and pull explicitly with worked examples, then test them.
Revisit push and pull words at the start of every lesson for retrieval.
Keep the digital work small: photo, video and one Book Creator page, so the science stays the focus.
flair: A class playground wall of toys that visitors can try.
Let each pair name their toy.
Visit the real school playground for a push and pull hunt.

directions.title: Force Investigators
directions.big_idea: Pushes and pulls are forces, and we can find out what they do by testing and recording.

lisc.intention: To investigate how pushes and pulls change how things move.
criteria: test a push and a pull and say what happened
record what I found with a photo, drawing or tally
say that a bigger push or pull makes a bigger change

assessment.title: Journal page
assessment.how: One drawn or photographed test per student in a Book Creator page; check for push or pull and what changed.

assessment.title: Observation checklist
assessment.how: Tick the class list as students predict, test and say what happened.

assessment.title: Show what we found
assessment.how: Pairs tell the class one finding using the sentence starter "When I pushed...".

arc.title: What Is a Force?
arc.summary: Feel pushes and pulls with ropes, balls and doors, and name them.

arc.title: Push and Pull Tests
arc.summary: Use simple fair tests: push a toy car, pull it with string.

arc.title: Magnets Pull
arc.summary: Explore magnets as a pull we cannot see.

arc.title: Balloon Power
arc.summary: Test balloons: what a push of air does to a toy.

arc.title: Ramps and Cars
arc.summary: Change the size of a push and measure how far a LEGO car goes.

arc.title: Record It
arc.summary: Photograph and film tests on the iPad and sort the results.

arc.title: Make a Prediction
arc.summary: Use what we know to predict a new test, then check.

arc.title: Force Findings
arc.summary: Share findings in a class Book Creator book.

resources.why: Ready-made cars, ramps and push and pull investigations for Foundation to Level 2.
Pulls we cannot see and pushes of air.
Photos and slow-motion video of tests.

connections.how: Pushing, pulling and moving in play links to the physical activity and movement the class already does.
Students listen to and describe sounds and movement, for example a fast push and a slow pull, as a short sound or rhythm.

pedagogy.how: Every lesson is a guided test with a question, a prediction and a result.
Predict and check questions open each test.
Each lesson starts by recalling the last finding.
Force, push, pull and magnet are taught explicitly.

backbone: Explicit teaching of fair testing with one worked example before pairs try.
Same routine each lesson: question, predict, test, record, say.
Check understanding with a quick show-me before moving on.
flair: A mystery box that moves on its own, for a hook.
Let students pick which toy car to test.
A scientist of the day role for each test.

directions.title: Robot Pushers
directions.big_idea: We can give a robot steps to follow so it pushes things where we want.

lisc.intention: To give a robot clear steps that make it push things where we want.
criteria: say a push moves something and a pull brings it closer
give a robot steps in the right order
test my steps and fix one mistake

assessment.title: Challenge photos
assessment.how: Photograph each pair's finished robot challenge; check the steps against the success criteria.

assessment.title: Observation checklist
assessment.how: Tick the class list as students give steps in order and fix a mistake.

assessment.title: Robot show
assessment.how: Pairs run their challenge for another pair and explain it.

arc.title: Robots Follow Steps
arc.summary: Be a robot: follow a friend's steps across the floor.

arc.title: Push or Pull?
arc.summary: Name pushes and pulls in play and see a robot push a block.

arc.title: Meet the Robot
arc.summary: Drive a Sphero with the iPad and notice how it pushes things.

arc.title: Steps in Order
arc.summary: Plan steps with arrow cards, then try them with the robot.

arc.title: Push the Block
arc.summary: Make the robot push a block to a target.

arc.title: Fix It
arc.summary: Find and fix a mistake in the steps.

arc.title: Challenge Course
arc.summary: Build a course with LEGO and push objects through it.

arc.title: Robot Show
arc.summary: Share the challenge and add a video to Book Creator.

resources.why: Robots that push objects and follow steps.
Drive the robots and record video.
Show the challenge with a video.

purchases.name: Bee-Bot or Blue-Bot floor robots
purchases.why: Simpler button-programmed robots may suit Foundation better than Sphero, and give each group a robot.

connections.how: Pushing, pulling and moving in play links to the physical activity and movement the class already does.
Students listen to and describe sounds and movement, for example a fast push and a slow pull, as a short sound or rhythm.

pedagogy.how: Students give a digital system ordered steps and fix mistakes.
James models stepping out an algorithm before pairs try.
Short guided turns with the robot before open challenges.
Steps, push, pull and fix are taught explicitly.

backbone: Unplugged first: students act as robots before using devices.
Model one set of steps with a worked example, then fade support.
Keep robot sessions short and structured to manage cognitive load.
Revisit the push and pull idea in every lesson so the science target is not lost.
flair: Name the robots and give them a story.
A class parade course for the final lesson.
Let students choose what the robot has to push.

choices.notes:
Being term 1, i need to embed PCMS/SWPBS in the lessons (Prep has a focus of "I show you and we practise together.") Here is the content that I need to touch on in age appropriate ways:  

PCMS / SWPBS Focus
Week 2
Classroom Expectations

LI: To behave safely and kindly in our specialist room.


Purpose from PCMS: When students know exactly what behaviour is expected of them, they are more likely to demonstrate these behaviours in the classroom. Teachers establish clear, consistent guidelines for conduct, which helps create a structured and positive learning environment.

Expectations to be taught:
Mini lesson / Task / Pack up
Toilet / drink
Out of bounds areas
Week 3
Classroom Procedures & Routines

LI: To follow routines so everyone can learn safely and calmly

Lesson starts off, do roll then practice transition to the basketball court during the first 10 mins of the lesson

Cut off class 10 mins early and heavy focus on transitions.

Purpose from PCMS: Procedures are the process for how things are done. When taught to fluency, they help students to form routines to efficiently and smoothly accomplish tasks. Teachers should implement these procedures because they minimise confusion and maximise instructional time.

Routines to be taught:
In-class transitions
Arriving & departing
Swapping over with other Specialists
Workbook expectations
Placement of personal belongings 
Week 4
Encouraging Expected Behaviour

Trial in term 1 working towards a Stamp Target

LI: To show behaviours that help everyone learn safely and happily in our specialist room.

Purpose from PCMS: To effectively recognise and encourage students when they display expected behaviours and to create a positive school environment where learning flourishes.

Expected behaviours to be taught/acknowledged:
Revise expectations from first week
Showing Kindness, Resilience and Responsibility
Classroom acknowledgement system (e.g. stamps for positive behaviours)
Give feedback at a 4:1 positive to corrective ratio (9:1 positive to corrective for students who may have experienced trauma)
Week 5
Discouraging Inappropriate Behaviour

Develop a pack for each Specialist class (Senior to Junior School) for students to reflect when removed.

LI: To respond calmly and respectfully when things go wrong in our Specialist room.

Purpose from PCMS: Specific corrective feedback is a necessary component of the learning process as students need to know when they have made an error and be redirected to the expected behaviour. Additionally, timely and constructive feedback prevents the escalation of negative behaviours, maintaining a conducive learning environment for all students.

School-wide sequence for minor behaviours:
Remind: A discreet reminder of the expected behaviour (1:1)
Redirect: Offer specific support or options to help the student re-engage (no more than two strategies)
Relocate: Move to a different seat or different class in PLT if behaviour continues, with follow-up reflection and communication as required
